content.text: {"relation":"REFINED","consensus_summary":"The blind consensus holds that being cast into the sea (stone, millstone, mountain) most commonly symbolizes complete, final, irreversible divine judgment or destruction — whatever sinks is gone beyond recovery. Alternatives include forgiveness of sins (Micah 7:19), faith moving mountains (Matt 21:21; Mark 11:23), warnings against causing stumbling, and a minority-to-common reading that the mountain/millstone represents a kingdom or empire (Babylon) overthrown, with the sea as the nations.","book_summary":"The book identifies the image specifically as the fall of Babylon: a ruling power irreversibly destroyed, sunk into the 'sea of peoples,' never to rise again. It treats the image as a phrase-symbol rather than a single-word symbol, citing Jer 51:63-64, Rev 18:21, and Ex 15:4-5.","consensus_core_identification":"Irreversible, total divine judgment/destruction — the sinking object signals permanent removal with no possibility of rising again, applied across persons, cities, kingdoms, and (in alternatives) sins or obstacles.","book_core_identification":"The irreversible destruction of a ruling power (paradigmatically Babylon), which sinks into the 'sea of peoples' never to rise — a specifically political-imperial judgment reading in which the sea represents the mass of nations/humanity.","core_relation":"BOOK_NARROWS","extension_relation":"BOOK_SUBSET","boundary_disagreement":"The book restricts the symbol to the overthrow of ruling powers/empires (the fall of Babylon), implicitly excluding cases the consensus admits under the same term: the forgiveness of sins cast into the sea (Micah 7:19), the faith-moves-mountains sayings (Matt 21:21; Mark 11:23), and the millstone warning about causing little ones to stumble (Matt 18:6). It also adds a specific interpretive gloss the consensus treats only as a minority/secondary view: the sea as the 'sea of peoples' (nations), rather than simply the abyss of oblivion.","material_contradiction":"","rationale":"The book's core preserves the consensus's central identification — irreversible destruction, never to rise — but narrows its referent to ruling powers, essentially elevating what Responses A and C list as an alternative (mountain/millstone = kingdom, sea = peoples/nations, applied to Babylon) into the primary and exclusive meaning. This is genuine boundary disagreement (the book excludes the sin-forgiveness, faith, and stumbling-warning applications from the symbol's extension) without replacing the central category of final, unrecoverable judgment. Hence REFINED with BOOK_NARROWS at the core and BOOK_SUBSET at the extension.","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"One could argue MATCH: the book's 'fall of Babylon' reading is exactly the dominant sense the consensus assigns to the key texts (Rev 18:21; Jer 51:63-64), and the consensus notes already acknowledge that judgment dominates for the stone/millstone passages, making the book's focus mere emphasis rather than material narrowing. Against this, the book's exclusive restriction to ruling powers and its distinctive 'sea of peoples' identification (the sea as nations, not mere oblivion) go beyond the consensus primary meaning and reclassify part of its extension, which fits REFINED better.","confidence":"high"}
